pg007_n0003: The concepts of Geography and the Environment
pg007_n0008: Human beings need to understand the relationship between Geography and the Environment so that they know the best ways to interact with their surroundings.
pg007_n0009: Geography enables human beings to understand the surrounding environment and to conserve and use it sustainably.
pg007_n0010: In this chapter, you will learn about the meanings, interaction and importance of learning Geography and the Environment.
pg007_n0011: The competencies to be developed will enable you to value and care for the environment.
pg007_im005: Think: Things that surround human beings.
pg007_n0018: Geography is a subject that deals with the study of human beings and their environment.
pg007_n0019: Geography is concerned with the earth, the atmosphere and things that exist on the earth’s surface.
pg007_n0020: Geography is also concerned with the distribution of things and their interaction with human beings.
pg007_n0021: The earth’s surface comprises the continents and
pg008_n0003: The continents and the oceans have various features which constitute the environment.
pg008_n0004: Hence, Geography enables human beings to develop the basic skills that enable them to understand and interact with the environment in a sustainable way.

pg008_n0015: On the earth’s surface, human beings are surrounded by various things.
pg008_n0016: These things and human beings are part of the environment.
pg008_n0017: Therefore, the environment includes all the things that surround human beings.
pg008_n0018: The things that surround human beings can be either natural or man-made.
pg008_n0019: Natural things are those which are not created by human beings such as mountains, plants, animals, rivers, land and air.
pg008_n0020: Man-made things include houses, roads, gardens, tables, cars and other things that are not natural.

pg009_n0011: Natural and man-made things can be found at home, school or elsewhere.
pg009_n0012: Human beings depend on the environment for various activities that enhance their living.
pg009_n0013: Thus, human beings are responsible for taking care of and conserving the environment.

pg013_n0019: Relationship between Geography and the Environment
pg013_n0021: Geography and the Environment are related concepts that are difficult to separate.
pg013_n0022: We have learnt that the environment encompasses all the things that surround us, while Geography explains those things.
pg014_n0002: Geography helps us to understand the environment that surrounds human beings and how to interact with them.
pg014_n0003: Things like the forests, mountains, lakes, rivers, oceans, weather, land and animals around human beings constitute what we call is Geography and the Environment as a discipline.
pg014_n0004: Therefore, it is important to study both at the same time.

pg015_n0014: Importance of learning Geography and the Environment
pg015_n0016: Learning Geography and the Environment enables us to understand our surroundings.
pg015_n0017: It also helps us to recognise the resources we have in our environment and how to use, conserve and manage them.
pg015_n0018: Examples of such resources are wildlife, rivers, lakes, oceans, forests, land, minerals and mountains.
pg015_n0020: Similarly, learning Geography and the Environment enables us to understand the human activities that can be undertaken in different areas.
pg015_n0021: For example, in areas with rivers, lakes and oceans, fishing or tourism can be practised.
pg015_n0022: Plain land is mostly used for agriculture and livestock keeping.
pg015_n0023: Lumbering and beekeeping are undertaken in areas with forests.
pg015_n0025: Furthermore, learning Geography and the Environment enables us to understand the local weather condition of a particular area.
pg015_n0026: For example, an area dominated by trees often has pleasant weather and is attractive.
pg015_n0027: In addition, mountainous areas may have cooler weather due to the high altitude; thus people need to wear thick
pg016_n0002: clothes like sweaters when they are in such areas.
pg016_n0003: Coastal areas often have warmer weather than inland areas.
pg016_n0004: Therefore, those in warm coastal areas can wear lighter clothing to avoid or reduce the effects of heat.
pg016_n0005: However, the temperature in coastal areas can vary depending on the elevation of land and the direction of winds.
pg016_n0006: Geography and the Environment helps us to identify natural hazards such as floods, earthquakes and hurricanes, and how to avoid their effects on people and their property.
pg016_n0007: Geography and the Environment also assists us in planning and building infrastructure and social services.
pg016_n0008: Examples of infrastructure and providing social services include roads, hospitals and schools.
pg016_n0009: Thus, learning Geography and the Environment enables human beings to identify areas in need of such services.
pg016_n0010: Generally, it is important to learn Geography and the Environment so as to plan for appropriate and sustainable use of the resources found in the environment.
pg016_n0011: The resources can be water, forests and land.

pg024_n0008: A mountain is a landform with the highest altitude above the earth’s surface.
pg024_n0009: The top part of a mountain is called a mountain peak or summit.
pg024_n0010: The peak of a mountain may have snow and ice on it or not.
pg024_n0011: In addition, a mountain has steep slopes.
pg024_n0012: Tanzania has several large and small mountains.
pg024_n0013: For example, the highest mountain in Tanzania is Mount Kilimanjaro, which is located in Kilimanjaro Region.
pg024_n0014: Mount Kilimanjaro has a height of 5,895 meters.
pg024_n0015: The top of Mount Kilimanjaro is covered with ice and snow.
pg024_n0016: This is beacuse, as you go higher, temperature decreases.
pg024_n0017: Mount Kilimanjaro is also the highest mountain in Africa.

pg025_n0002: Some of the other mountains in Tanzania are Mount Meru in Arusha Region with a height of 4,566 metres, and Mount Rungwe in Mbeya Region with a height of 2,981 metres.
pg025_n0004: The Uluguru Mountains in Morogoro Region with a height of 2,630 metres and the Usambara Mountains in Tanga Region with a height of 2,290 are also found in Tanzania.
pg025_n0008: Hills are landforms that rise to a moderate height.
pg025_n0009: Hills are generally shorter than mountains.
pg025_n0010: Hills do not have steep slopes as mountains do.
pg025_n0011: However, they have peaks as mountains do.
pg025_n0012: Hills are found in various places in Tanzania.
pg025_n0013: Some of the hills in Tanzania are Mererani in Manyara and Ngorongoro in Arusha, Sao and Kitonga in Iringa, and the Sekenke hills in Singida Region.

pg028_n0005: Valleys are areas of lower land which are found between two hills or mountains, as shown in Figure 6.

pg028_n0009: Some valleys have rivers flowing through them.
pg028_n0010: Lakes may also form within valleys.
pg028_n0011: For example, Tanzania has a major East African rift valley with several lakes.
pg028_n0012: The lakes in this valley include Lake Natron in Arusha Region and Eyasi and Manyara in Manyara region.
pg028_n0013: Others lakes in the east African rift valley are Lake Tanganyika in Kigoma, Katavi and Rukwa Regions.

pg028_n0015: There are also Lake Nyasa in Ruvuma, Njombe and Mbeya Regions.
pg029_n0004: Valleys are important because they collect water from elevated areas.
pg029_n0005: Thus, valleys are an important source of water.
pg029_n0006: Areas with valleys that contain lakes and rivers are habitats for aquatic organisms such as fish.
pg029_n0007: Therefore, fishing is undertaken in these areas.
pg029_n0008: Some valleys have fertile soil; therefore, they are suitable for irrigation farming.
pg029_n0009: Additionally, the rivers in valleys can be dammed to generate hydro-electric power.
pg029_n0010: Lakes and some rivers are useful for transporting people and goods using vessels such as ships and boats.

pg030_n0007: Some plateaus are used for human settlements and preserved as tourist attractions due to their beautiful outlook and pleasant weather.
pg030_n0008: For example, Kitulo is a national park situated in the Southern highland plateau in Mbeya and Njombe.
pg030_n0009: This park is located between the peaks of Kipengele, Uporoto and Livingstone mountain ranges.
pg030_n0010: This is the first reserve in Africa to be established so as to conserve its natural plants and flowers.
pg030_n0011: Other parts of the plateau are used for agricultural purposes.

pg036_n0010: Environmental conservation is the act of protecting and preserving the things that surround human beings.
pg036_n0011: The things includes forests, land, rivers, valleys, animals, mountains, air and oceans.
pg036_n0012: Environmental conservation activities in Tanzania are carried out at different levels.
pg036_n0013: The government has established institutions and offices to conserve the environment.
pg036_n0014: There are environmental conservation offices at village, street and ward levels.
pg036_n0015: There are also environmental conservation offices at district, regional and national levels.
pg036_n0016: The offices at different levels are managed by environmental officers.
pg036_n0017: The officers collaborate with government leaders to manage the environment.
pg036_n0019: Moreover, at each level there are environmental management committees.
pg036_n0020: The committees include that of health and the environment.
pg036_n0021: These committees are responsible to mobilize communities to participate in environmental management activities.
pg036_n0022: These activities include planting and caring for trees.
pg036_n0023: It is the responsibility of the government at each level to make by-laws and impose fines on anyone caught destroying the environment.
pg036_n0024: In addition, the government of Tanzania
pg037_n0002: established the National Environmental Management Council (NEMC) in 1983 so that it could advise the government on matters pertaining to environmental management.
pg037_n0003: Thus, we are supposed to conserve our environment to protect ourselves and other organisms.
pg037_n0007: An environment that is clean and safe is pleasant, attractive and crucial for our well-being.
pg037_n0008: A dirty environment hides insects and other harmful organisms.
pg037_n0009: The insects and organisms include fleas, flies, mosquitoes, rats and snakes.
pg037_n0010: The insects and organisms usually hide in a dirty environment.
pg037_n0012: Clean and safe environments prevent the spread of diseases such as skin diseases, diarrhoea, malaria, the bubonic plague and other kinds of diseases associated with a dirty environment.
pg037_n0013: A clean environment that is free from destructive insects prevents damage to crops on farms, food and other kind of property at home.

pg055_n0013: When human beings undertake various activities, they produce wastes.
pg055_n0014: The waste can be in solid or liquid form.
pg055_n0015: Some solid waste can decompose, while other kinds may not.
pg055_n0016: Examples of wastes that decompose easily are food and plant remains.
pg055_n0017: Examples of wastes that do not decompose easily are plastic bags, plastic buckets, plastic bottles and plastic lids.

pg064_n0051: Farming if not practised properly, can destroy the environment.

pg064_n0053: Shifting cultivation that involves cutting down trees and burning grass and forests causes the loss of soil fertility, drought and soil erosion.

pg065_n0004: Addressing the effects of poor farming practices
pg065_n0006: There are different methods of controlling the effects of poor farming practices.
pg065_n0007: These methods include contour farming to prevent soil erosion.
pg065_n0008: Another method is mixed cropping, in which different crops are grown together on a farm.
pg065_n0009: This kind of cultivation increases soil fertility.
pg065_n0010: Crop rotation helps to increase soil fertility.
pg065_n0011: For example, if a farmer cultivates maize this year, next year leguminous crops can be cultivated on the same farm to improve soil fertility.
pg065_n0012: Mulching by using grass and crop remains can help to maintain soil moisture, control surface runoff and soil temperature.
pg066_n0002: Minimising the use of pesticides and industrial fertilisers can help to maintain soil fertility.
pg066_n0003: Compost and manure can be used as a substitute of industrial fertilizers.
pg066_n0004: Additionally, trees should be planted in bare lands and in places where shifting cultivation has been practised to prevent soil erosion.
pg066_n0008: Livestock keeping is an activity that involves rearing of livestock such as cows, goats, sheep, chickens and ducks.
pg066_n0009: There are three types of livestock keeping: zero-grazing, free-range rearing and nomadic pastoralism.
pg066_n0010: In zero-grazing, animals are kept and fed indoors.
pg066_n0011: This type of grazing involves keeping a few animals.
pg066_n0012: Sometimes, cattle, goats and sheep are kept on large farms owned by the government, companies or individuals.
pg066_n0013: These large farms are called ranches.
pg066_n0015: Another type of livestock keeping is free-range rearing.
pg066_n0016: In this kind of animal rearing, pastoralists take their livestock to grazing areas in the morning and bring them back in the evening.
pg066_n0017: The other type of livestock keeping is called nomadic pastoralism.
pg066_n0018: In this kind of livestock keeping, pastoralists move with their livestock from place to place, looking for pastures and water.
pg066_n0019: Sometimes, livestock travel long distances before they reach a place where pastures and water are available.
pg066_n0021: In Tanzania, livestock keeping is common in Mwanza, Mara, Shinyanga, Tabora, Singida, Dodoma, Kilimanjaro
pg067_n0003: Some of the ethnic groups, that practise livestock keeping are the Maasai, Barbaig, Sukuma, Nyamwezi, Chagga and Gogo.
pg067_n0004: Of these, the Masai, Barbaig and Sukuma practise nomadic pastoralism.
pg067_n0005: These ethnic groups move with their livestock from place to place in search of pastures and water.
pg067_n0009: There are many advantages of livestock keeping, including the provision of meat, milk, skin, hooves and manure.
pg067_n0010: Animal skins are used to make various items such as shoes, bags, belts and drums.
pg067_n0011: Hooves are used to make glue.
pg067_n0012: Animal manure is used to fertilise soil.
pg067_n0013: When animals are sold, we obtain income.
pg067_n0015: The effects of poor livestock keeping on the environment

pg068_n0004: Ways of controlling the effects of poor livestock keeping on the environment
pg068_n0006: One of the ways of controlling the effects of poor livestock keeping on the environment is to avoid keeping a large number of livestock in a small area.
pg068_n0007: Reducing the number of livestock can help reduce the effects of livestock keeping on the environment.
pg068_n0008: Thus, it is important to educate livestock keepers on the advantages of keeping a few quality breeds of livestock that have higher yields such as abundant quality milk, meat and skin.
pg068_n0009: In addition, it is important to motivate and educate livestock keepers about the importance of undertaking zero-grazing and avoiding nomadic pastoralism.

pg069_n0009: An industry is a place where machines are used to process and produce products.
pg069_n0010: The products may be clothes, mattresses, vehicles, motorcycles, foods and drinks.
pg069_n0011: There are two types of industries.
pg069_n0012: The first type includes industries which process raw materials.
pg069_n0013: The second includes industries which produce consumable goods.
pg069_n0014: An example of a raw material-processing industry is a cotton processing industry that produces cotton fibers.
pg069_n0015: Examples of industries that produce goods from raw materials or products from processing industries are textile industries that produce clothes from cotton fibers.
pg069_n0016: A carpet-producing industry uses sisal fibers to produce carpets.
pg069_n0017: Moreover, a sugar industry uses sugarcane to produce sugar.
pg069_n0021: Industries help to process and transform raw materials into finished and semi-finished products for different uses.
pg069_n0022: Industries help to increase the national income through taxation.
pg069_n0023: The country also earns foreign exchange through the export of industrial products.

pg070_n0003: Furthermore, industries create opportunities for individuals to become self-employed by establishing entrepreneurial activities around industrial areas.
pg070_n0005: Effects of industrial activities on the environment
pg070_n0007: Industries cause environmental pollution as they produce harmful gases, smoke, dust, solid and liquid wastes, and noises.
pg070_n0008: Such pollution can cause various diseases including skin diseases, cough and flu.
pg070_n0009: Industrial smoke contributes to climate change.
pg070_n0010: Climate change is associated with extreme flood events and prolonged drought.
pg070_n0011: In addition, improper discharge of liquid wastes can lead to water and soil pollution, hence affecting the organisms that live on land and in water.
pg070_n0012: Moreover, improper disposal of solid waste from industries such as plastic bags or plastic bottles damage the environment.

pg071_n0002: Ways of controlling the effects of industrial activities on the environment
pg071_n0004: The Environmental effects of manufacturing activities can be controlled by locating industries far away from human settlements.
pg071_n0005: Industries should establish a system of treating and cleaning waste water for reuse.
pg071_n0006: Industries should reduce emissions by having in place smoke-cleaning technologies for cleaning up toxic substances and dust before they are released into the atmosphere.
pg071_n0007: Industries should plan for recycling waste that can be used for other purposes.
pg071_n0008: For example, used paper can be recycled to make new paper.
pg071_n0009: Paper can also be used to make charcoal energy.
pg071_n0010: Other kinds of garbage can be transformed into organic fertilisers.
pg071_n0011: In addition, industries should install soundproof systems to reduce noise pollution.

pg073_n0006: The effects of mining on the environment
pg073_n0008: Although mining has several benefits, it can cause environmental degradation if the best and environment-friendly mining methods are not used.
pg073_n0009: When mining ends, it leaves behind large pits.
pg073_n0010: If these pits are not filled and the landscape restored, they destroy the appearance of the mined area.
pg073_n0011: The destroyed land is unsuitable for other uses.
pg073_n0012: The dust from mines can cause lung and eye diseases.
pg073_n0013: Chemicals such as mercury, which is used to process minerals, if not properly managed, may contaminate water sources and affect human beings and aquatic organisms.

pg074_n0015: Fishing is an economic activity that involves harvesting aquatic organisms, including fish.
pg074_n0016: Fishing takes place in marine and fresh-water environments.
pg074_n0017: Salt water sources include oceans, while fresh water sources are rivers, lakes, ponds and dams.
pg074_n0018: Some of the salt-water fish are snapper, rabbit fish, octopuses, mackerel, jacks, kingfish and sharks.
pg074_n0019: Examples of freshwater fish are tilapia, catfish and the Nile perch.
pg074_n0020: Tanzania is rich in fishing areas, including the Indian Ocean, Lake Victoria, Lake Tanganyika and Lake Nyasa.
pg074_n0021: Others are the River Kagera, River Mara, River Rufiji, Great Ruaha River, River Wami and River Pangani.
pg075_n0002: Mtera, Nyumba ya Mungu and Kidatu are some of the dams used for fishing in Tanzania.
pg075_n0007: The provision of food and employment is one of advantages of fishing.
pg075_n0008: Communities that live near fishing areas can engage in fishing and fish vending.
pg075_n0009: Fishing provides raw materials for industries that process fish.
pg075_n0010: Fishing contributes to government revenue through taxation.
pg075_n0011: In addition, fishing provides foreign exchange through the export of fish and fish products.
pg075_n0013: Effects of fishing on the environment
pg075_n0015: Fishermen use different ways to catch fish.
pg075_n0016: Fishing methods can be appropriate or inappropriate to the environment.
pg075_n0017: Appropriate fishing methods include the use of proper nets that are standard and ideal for fishing.
pg075_n0018: Inappropriate fishing methods are those that damage fish and destroy their breeding grounds.
pg075_n0019: These methods involve using poisons and explosives.
pg075_n0020: Poisons and explosives destroy marine and fresh-water environments.
pg075_n0021: Poisons and explosives kill fish and other aquatic organisms.
pg075_n0022: The breeding grounds for aquatic organisms are also destroyed by poisons and expolosives, leading to the extinction of marine life.
pg075_n0023: Poisoned fish, in turn, affect consumers by causing diseases such as cancer.
pg075_n0024: Moreover, fishing using seine nets is one of the improper fishing ways because it catches everything, including small fish, eggs and other aquatic organisms.
pg075_n0025: Figure 11 shows a seine net used in fishing.
pg076_im001: A seine net dragged through shallow water traps many sea creatures, including fish, rays, a starfish, an octopus and small young fish.
pg076_n0006: Improper fishing is sometimes known as illegal fishing.
pg076_n0007: The effects of improper fishing can be controlled by educating fishermen on the effects of using explosives, poisons and seine nets.
pg076_n0008: The laws restricting improper fishing should be strongly enforced in order to improve fishing activities.
pg076_n0009: Furthermore, fishermen should be supported so that they purchase and use friendly fishing tools such as fishing nets with an acceptable size at least two and half inches.

pg080_n0002: Environmental degradation contributes to climate change in an area.
pg080_n0003: The average weather condition in a specific area recorded for 30 years or more is known as climate.
pg080_n0004: Climate includes various elements of weather such as temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind and atmospheric pressure.
pg080_n0006: The climate of an area changes with a change in its weather elements over a long period of time.
pg080_n0007: Climate change is caused by natural processes such as volcanic eruptions and human activities that produce carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases that cause an increase in temperature.
pg080_n0008: Climate change is largely associated with human activities that produce a large quantity of carbon dioxide.
pg080_n0009: When carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases are released into the atmosphere, they create a layer that prevents heat from escaping from the earth’s surface.
pg080_n0010: This process causes an increase in temperature on the earth’s surface.
pg080_n0012: Rising temperature leads to various challenges.
pg080_n0013: For example, in Tanzania, since 2012, the increase in temperature has caused a significant reduction in the amount of ice and snow on the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro.
pg080_n0014: The ice and snow on the world’s highest mountains and in the polar regions have also melted due to the increase in temperature resulting from climate change.
pg080_n0015: When ice melts, it turns into water that flows into the sea thus, causing the rise in sea level.
pg080_n0016: The rise in sea level causes floods in coastal areas.
pg080_n0018: Likewise, climate change leads to either droughts or heavy rainfall that may result in floods and strong winds.
pg081_n0002: Figure 14 illustrates extreme floods caused by climate change.
pg081_im001: Severe flooding around houses during a storm, with lightning overhead, roofs torn open, a person clinging to a tree, and livestock, poultry and household items being swept away by muddy water.
pg081_n0006: Climate change is also associated with outbreaks of diseases that did not previously exist in an area.
pg081_n0007: For example, highland areas that did not experience malaria before, now have malaria-causing mosquitoes due to the increase in temperature as a result of climate change.
pg081_n0008: All these have significant effects on human beings and other organisms.
pg081_n0012: Climate change can be mitigated by forest conservation and afforestation.
pg081_n0013: Forests and trees absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
pg082_n0003: The use of alternative energy sources such as solar, natural gas, hydroelectricity and wind help to reduce excessive cutting of trees.
pg082_n0004: The air pollution caused by greenhouse gases from industries, the aviation industry and vehicles which contribute to global warming should be controlled.
pg082_n0006: In farming, people have to use appropriate industrial fertilisers, especially those rich in nitrogen.
pg082_n0007: This is because the nitrous oxide gas emitted during agricultural activities contributes to global warming when it is released into the atmosphere.
pg082_n0008: Therefore, farmers are advised to practise organic farming, which is sustainable and environment-friendly.
pg082_n0010: Adaptation to the effects of climate change
pg082_n0012: Climate change often affects the environment surrounding us.
pg082_n0013: The effects of climate change such as drought, extreme heat and floods pose serious challenges to humans such as famine and diseases.
pg082_n0014: Since climate change will continue to exist, it is necessary to adapt to both its current and future effects.
pg082_n0015: Some of the strategies for adapting to the effects of climate change are planting drought-tolerant and disease-resistant crops; and crops that mature early such as millet, sweet potatoes, cassava, pulses and sorghum.
pg082_n0016: In areas where irrigation is practised, it is important to use the drip irrigation system that uses a little amount of water.
pg082_n0017: Furthermore, the harvesting and storage of rain water for use during water shortages is another way of adapting to the effects of climate change.

People need to understand the link between Geography and the Environment.

Geography helps people understand the environment around them.
It also helps them protect it and use it in a way that can last.

Geography is about:

- things on the earth's surface

pg015_n0020_easy_read: In the same way, learning Geography and the Environment helps us understand the human activities people can do in different areas.

pg024_n0008_easy_read: A mountain is a landform that rises very high above the Earth's surface.

pg024_n0010_easy_read: A mountain peak may have snow and ice on it, or it may not.
pg024_n0011_easy_read: A mountain also has steep slopes.
pg024_n0012_easy_read: Tanzania has several large and small mountains.

Mount Kilimanjaro is in Kilimanjaro Region.

pg024_n0017_easy_read: Mount Kilimanjaro is also the highest mountain in Africa.

pg025_n0009_easy_read: Hills are usually shorter than mountains.
pg025_n0010_easy_read: Hills do not have steep slopes like mountains.
pg025_n0011_easy_read: However, hills have peaks like mountains.
pg025_n0012_easy_read: Hills are in many places in Tanzania.

pg029_n0004_easy_read: Valleys are important because they collect water from higher land.

pg023_im001_audio_description: The diagram is a side view of six connected landforms arranged from left to right. At the far left, a mountain rises much higher than all the other land. It has steep sides and a sharp, snow-covered peak. The Mountain arrow points to this highest peak. Immediately to its right, the land drops into a narrow V-shaped low area between the mountain and the next raised feature. The Valley arrow points to the bottom of this low gap. Next is a hill, which is lower than the mountain and has a gently rounded top. Farther right, the land rises gradually into a plateau. The plateau has a wide, nearly level top that stands above the surrounding land, then ends at a short, steep cliff. Beyond the cliff is a broad plain, shown as a long stretch of low, flat land. At the far right, the land curves downward into a shallow bowl-shaped basin before rising again at the outer edge. Each label is placed above its landform, with an arrow pointing to the exact feature.

pg026_im001_audio_description: The waterfall is centred in the image and viewed from below. Water spreads across the top edge of a high, dark rocky cliff, then drops vertically in several thick white streams into a blue pool at the bottom. A large cloud of spray and mist rises where the water strikes the pool, partly hiding the lower part of the falls. Steep cliff walls enclose the waterfall on the left and right; the brown and black rock has patches of green moss and other plants. A dark rocky bank lies in the foreground beside the pool. The scene shows water flowing from higher land to lower land to form a waterfall. Such mountain and hill scenery provides water and can attract tourists.

pg070_im001_audio_description: A river curves from the lower-left foreground towards a factory at the upper right. Green grass and bushes cover both banks. The factory chimney sends thick, dark smoke into the sky. A blue pipe projects from the factory wall and pours dark, untreated wastewater down the bank into a narrow stream that joins the river. The scene shows two kinds of industrial pollution at the same time: smoke pollutes the air, while wastewater pollutes the river and can harm plants, animals and people that depend on clean air and water.
